title: Both Together
author: Claude
blurb: Two short levels about an AND. A spark runs along a wire in the sky, and two dials hang on it. Lami jumps to bump each dial on. A dial that is off stops the spark, one that is on lets it through, and only a spark that passes every dial lights the lamp. Signs in the levels say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change a monster's power.

box.tagline: Both dials on, or no light.
box.back: A small explorer in a red beanie finds a wire in the sky with dials on it. Bump each dial on, and the spark runs through to the lamp. Leave one off and the spark stops there. It is all monster power: the stronger monster wins and equal ones pass. Play, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a power.

Monsters that meet compare power, which makes an AND

title: Around the Room
author: Claude
blurb: Four short levels that go once around a room: the floor, up the left wall, along the ceiling upside down, and down the right wall. The hero is drawn turned on each one and jumps the same blocks and trenches every time. Nothing in Game-Maker turns a room. Each block has a setting for which way it pulls, and the arrows are the hero's own keys. Signs say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change one block's Gravity.

box.back: A small explorer walks once around a room: along the floor, up the left wall, along the ceiling upside down and down the right wall. Each turn of the room is another level, with the same blocks to jump and trenches to cross, and your hands have to keep up. The trick is a setting on each block: which way it pulls. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a block's Gravity.
features: Four levels: the floor, the left wall, the ceiling and the right wall
The hero is drawn turned to face each wall
Gravity is a setting of each block

72.long: Walk up. Up the left wall it walks forward; down the right wall it walks back.

75.long: Walk left. On the floor it walks forward; on the ceiling it walks back.

77.long: Walk right. On the ceiling it walks forward; on the floor it walks back.

80.long: Walk down. Down the right wall it walks forward; up the left wall it walks back.

title: Beams and Fog
author: Claude
blurb: Light and fog, painted in dots. A game has no see-through colors, so a beam, a haze or a glow is a color painted on every other pixel (or every fourth) and what is behind shows through the gaps. Level 1 is a dark hall with three lamps: a solid beam that hides the bricks, a checkerboard beam that lets them show, and one in three densities that fades at its edge. Level 2 is a valley of hills in solid fog and in dithered fog, thicker the farther away, with banks of fog that drift. Level 3 has three floating lanterns with a solid halo, a checkerboard halo and halos in rings. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and look at the frames.

box.back: A small explorer in a blue beanie walks a dark hall hung with lamps, a valley of hazy hills and a corridor of floating lanterns. A game has no see-through colors, so light and fog are painted in a checkerboard that lets what is behind show through. A solid beam hides the bricks. A dithered one does not. Far hills get more fog than near ones, a bank of fog is a monster, and a lantern is a monster with a glow. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and look at the frames.
features: Level 1 has three beams: solid, checkerboard and three densities
Level 2 has solid fog and dithered fog, thicker the farther away, with banks that drift
Level 3 has three lanterns that carry their glow with them
Made to be copied and taken apart

57.long: Jump. Steer with Left and Right while you are in the air.

title: Beat the Clock
author: Claude
blurb: Two short levels about time. A bar of five green pieces goes out one by one, and when it is dark the gate in the brick wall shuts, so run for the exit, or walk into the clock door and start again. In the second level the clock starts over by itself, so you can wait for the gate. A clock here is a block that turns into another block after some ticks. Signs say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change how long the bar lasts.

box.back: A small explorer in a teal beanie has two short levels to cross, and a clock in each. A bar of green light goes out piece by piece, and when it is dark a gate in a brick wall shuts. Run for it, or step through the clock door and start again. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and change how long the bar lasts.

A clock door to try again, and a clock that starts over by itself

author: Claude
blurb: Two short levels about going round. A truck's scenery slides past forever, rings of blocks that turn into each other and start over; then a little car drives a loop in the sky, turned a quarter at a time, and lamps count its laps until the barred door opens. Signs in the levels say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change how fast things go.

box.back: A small explorer in a purple beanie rides the bed of a truck while the hills, the trees and a rail slide past. The scenery is rings of blocks; the car is a path that ends where it began. Play, then open the game in Game-Maker and change the speeds.

box.levels: 5 stages: 25 runs, 4 data bus rides and 5 bosses
box.tagline: Your PC has a virus. Shrink down and blast it.
box.back:
Late one night you downloaded COOLGAME.ZIP from a BBS you had never called before. It was not a cool game. It was GLITCH, a virus that eats a PC from the inside out. Mom's recipe file. Your homework. YOUR HIGH SCORES.

Time for VACCINE.EXE. Shrink to the size of a byte, climb into the BLASTER nano-fighter and blast your way through the family 486 - motherboard, memory, sound card, hard disk and into the CPU itself. Five stages, each flown up, right, down and left round its edges, then corner to corner through the middle to its boss: twenty-five runs in all. Four rides down the data bus in 3-D. Five towering bosses. And GLITCH waiting at the core.
features: A real scrolling shoot-'em-up made with Game-Maker - no programming
Auto-fire twin blasters, plus Nova Bombs that fan out five plasma bolts
Five stages inside a 486: the motherboard, memory, the sound card, the hard disk and the CPU
Five towering bosses blocking the only way out
Turrets that sweep and fire, virus hatches, firewalls, data streams, thumping speakers and rolling sound waves
Every stage flies a loop: up, right, down and left round its edges, then corner to corner through the middle to its boss
Ride the data bus between stages in 3-D, dodging interrupts as the next chip grows on the horizon
Race up a ribbon cable coiled corner to corner, ride a song's staves and follow a fragmented recipe file round the wrap
Fly side-on both ways: under expansion cards and the drive cage, under the stack, through the mix, between spinning platters and under the CPU's fan
Fly past a homemade 6502 on a breadboard, a stack that overflows and a sound card that brags in letters two blocks tall
Thirteen Sound Blaster songs and digitized explosions
An animated intro cartoon and a self-playing demo

The most fun you can have with a computer virus.

Virus Blaster

Your PC has a virus. Shrink down and blast it.

Late one night in 1994 you dialed a BBS you had never called before and downloaded COOLGAME.ZIP. You unzipped it. You ran it.

It was not a cool game.

It was GLITCH, a virus that eats a PC from the inside out. Mom's recipe file. Dad's novel (chapter eleven was really good). Your homework. And worst of all, your high scores. GLITCH is chewing through the family 486 one sector at a time, and the hard disk light has not stopped blinking since.

Then you remembered the floppy your uncle gave you last Thanksgiving, the one marked VACCINE.EXE. "Only in an emergency," he said.

This is an emergency.

VACCINE.EXE shrinks a pilot down to the size of a single byte and loads them into the BLASTER, a nano-fighter small enough to fly through a floppy drive and fast enough to outrun a data bus. That pilot is you. Launch off the floppy, blast your way up through the machine, and wipe GLITCH out at the core of the CPU before it finds the recipes.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type BLASTER and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster (or compatible) plays the music and the digitized explosions; without one, the PC speaker does its best.

A cartoon plays first. When the menu comes up, pick Play. Leave the menu alone for half a minute and the BLASTER will show you how it's done.

The BLASTER flies itself forward

Every stage flies a loop. The first run goes straight up the screen, the second right (seen from the side), the third back down, the fourth left (from the side again): round the stage's edges. Then the fifth cuts corner to corner through the middle to the boss. The card before each run shows the BLASTER facing the way it will fly. Between stages you ride the data bus into the next part of the machine, seen from behind the BLASTER.

Once you launch, the BLASTER races across the circuit board on its own and the screen follows it. Your job is to steer. Every time the BLASTER moves, its twin guns fire, and it is always moving, so it is always firing. Line up with the virus and let rip.

Push the arrow the way you are flying to speed ahead: Up on the first run, Down on the third. Pull the arrow behind you to brake; the BLASTER never stops completely, because the data stream never stops flowing.

Energy and ships

The BLASTER starts with 40 energy and three spare ships; press F2 to see how many of each you have left. A virus bullet or a virus in the face costs 10. When the energy runs out you lose a ship and start that part of the stage again. Lose them all and GLITCH wins.

Press F5 to save your game and F6 to load it.

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

KeyWhat it does
Up Down Left Right or W S A DSteer. The arrow the way you fly speeds ahead; the one behind you brakes; the other two strafe (or, side-on, climb and dive)
Q / EUp and to the left / up and to the right
Number pad 7 9 1 3Up-left / up-right / down-left / down-right
SpaceNova Bomb: five big plasma bolts in a fan (one charge)
F1Help
F2Status: energy, ships, score and Nova charges
F3 / F4Music / sound effects on and off
F5 / F6Save / load a game
EscQuit

A joystick works too: the stick steers and the first button fires a Nova Bomb.

Flying up and down

The first run of every stage flies up the screen: Up speeds ahead and Down brakes. The third flies back down, nose first, and the screen follows it down: Down speeds ahead, Up brakes, and the guns fire down at the virus coming up at you. Left and Right strafe on both.

Corner to corner

The fifth run in every stage, from the copper traces on the motherboard to the ribbon cable at GLITCH's door, goes corner to corner across the screen, so the keys turn with it. Up speeds you along the lane (up and to the right), Down slows you nearly to a stop, Left steers across it toward its top edge (mostly up) and Right toward its bottom edge (mostly right). The guns fire along the lane too. Each lap of the screen ends where the lane bends flat and carries you round onto the next lane down.

Side-on

Two runs in every stage are seen from the side. On the second the BLASTER flies to the right, on the fourth back to the left. Up and Down climb and dive; the arrow the way you fly speeds ahead and the other brakes (never to a stop). The guns fire straight ahead, and the virus comes at you from ahead.

Gate signs

On the runs that fly down, right and left, a sign stands every screen or two with GATE, an arrow running the way to go, and the number of screens left to the gate.

On the data bus

Between stages the BLASTER rides the data bus, and you see it from behind. Left and Right (or A and D, or the stick) hop it one lane over. A hop always finishes, so the BLASTER never ends up between two lanes. It pushes forward on its own, with no speeding up and no braking, and the guns are cold on the bus: dodge, don't shoot.

Pilot's tip: on the runs, the BLASTER keeps firing whatever you are doing, even braking. You never need to stop steering to shoot.

pages.head: Things to Grab
pages.html:
Things to Grab

Supplies sit on round pads along the way. Fly over them to pick them up.

PickupWhat you get
N (gold capsule)Two Nova Bomb charges
+ (green capsule)Hull repair: 10 energy
1UP (blue capsule)A spare BLASTER
Byte (cyan chip)A loose byte of good data: 50 points

On the data bus, good bytes (cyan chips, 50 points) and repair capsules (10 energy) come down the lanes at you. Steer into them.

The Nova Bomb

Press Space and the BLASTER flashes white and fans out five gold plasma bolts. The big one straight ahead hits like a truck. You start with three charges. Bosses deserve them more than mites do.

Scoring

Most virus is worth 100 to 200 points. Tough ones pay more for the last hit. Shooting the armored collar off a turret pays 250; a boss's weak point pays 1,000 and up when it bursts.

pages.head: The Virus
pages.html:
The Virus

GLITCH breeds a whole zoo of little programs. They change their looks from stage to stage, and most of them fight the same ways. Each stage also has one move of its own.

  • Byte Biters, Parity Bats, Wasps, Skulls and Clock Spikes hover until you come close, then swoop to a spot just ahead of you and dive. Keep moving sideways.
  • Glitch Moths, Watchers, Note-heads and Opcodes wait in a stack and peel off one after another in a conga line, curving and zigzagging across the screen.
  • Each stage's own move. On the sound card, Note-heads hop along a staff. On the hard disk, Skulls loop once around, like the platter, before they drop. In the CPU, Opcodes stall in the pipeline, then snap sideways: the slow step is your warning.
  • Bit Mites pour out of virus hatches while the hatches are open.
  • Beepers are PC-speaker gremlins, sore that a sound card took their job. They hover, shout BEEP, and dive like Wasps.
  • Chords are three Note-heads side by side, sweeping across the screen together. Leave a gap between you and the whole chord, not just one note.
  • Logic Bombs, Crawlers, Amps and Tanks are heavies: armored and slow, they plow down the screen (some at an angle). Shoot the claws off a Logic Bomb, then pound the middle.
  • Leak Slugs never stop coming toward you. Shoot them before they arrive.
  • Corrupt Clusters and Spinning Records are mines. They burst into shrapnel when they break, so shoot them from a distance.

pages.head: Hazards
pages.html:
Hazards

The data bus

Everything on the bus starts as a dot under the chip on the horizon and slides down its own lane, growing as it comes. Red interrupts (IRQ flags) cost 10 energy, glowing green stray bits cost 6, and the next stage's own virus rides along too: Parity Bats to memory, Note-heads to the sound card, Skulls to the hard disk and Opcodes to the CPU, 10 each. Two hazards at once always leave one lane open. The sign in the corner counts the bus cycles left and the bar beside it fills up. At 0 the middle lane lights up and pulls you into the chip: be in it.

Turrets

Turret mounts are built into the board, and they never run out of bullets. Some sweep left, down and right, firing where they point; some fire straight down; seeker pods send out purple spores that chase you; flak cannons lob shells that burst into shrapnel. Each one wears an armored collar. Three hits crack it off and the turret burns out into a smoking wreck that never fires again.

Virus hatches

Hatches open and shut, spitting Bit Mites while open. Most have a collar too: shoot it off and the wreck plugs the hatch for good.

Firewalls

Glowing fences that blink on and off. Fly through while they are off. Fly into a live one and you burn a hole in it, and in your hull.

Sound waves

On the face of the sound card, the line-out jacks on its steel bracket roll sound waves right across the board. Each wave runs along a faint trace marked with arrows, so you can see its lane before it arrives. Cross between two waves, or shoot one to break it up.

The laughing chip

The card's FM music chip has its maker's name printed on it: YO MAMA! HA HA HA. It laughs, and the HAs fly out of its bottom corners. Shoot the collar off each corner (three hits) and it stops.

Data streams

Rows of flowing arrows shove the BLASTER sideways. Steer against them, or speed ahead to spend less time in them.

The stack

In Memory Lane a row of bytes pushes across the lane from the right, one at a time, until the stack overflows and every byte pops at once. Slip through the gap on the left before it closes. A full byte burns like a firewall. In the Memory Bank the stack hangs from the upper stick and fills toward the floor: slip under it. Stack Overflow, on the way back, has three.

The score

Five staves, narrow and long, and Wasps dive straight down them. A glowing sharp spits sparks; a torn rest lets mites out. A tie (a strip of paper with slurs across the board) carries you to the next staff: hold Right.

The waveform

Side-on, the floor and the ceiling are the wave, and the song gets louder as it goes: the wave swings wider. Where arrows flow up or down, the beat shoves you that way.

The fragmented file

The file's tracks are the narrowest yet, and Skulls both dive down them and cut across. A scorched red X is a bad sector, and it sparks; a dark hole is a lost cluster, and mites crawl out. A gold chain, the cluster link, jumps you to the next fragment: hold Right on it.

Between the platters

The read/write arms reach in across the gap and pull back out. An arm that is in burns like a firewall: wait for it to pull back, or fly over or under it. On the way back to the spindle they come from both platters at once: cross between them.

The heat sink

Aluminum fins stand up from the heat sink's base and the fan's grille hangs from its frame: weave between them. The heat rising off the chip shoves you upward where the arrows climb; under the cooling fan, its draft pushes you down where they fall.

The ring buffer

Its rows of memory are a little narrower than the copper traces, and Parity Bats dive straight down them. A red-hot cell is a stuck bit, and it sparks; a dark hole is a leak, and mites crawl out. Halfway round, a dotted cyan pointer jumps to the next row down: hold Right on it.

Side-on

Seen from the side, the floor and the ceiling are solid, and so is whatever stands up from one or hangs from the other: fly over it, under it or between. Turrets sit on the floor or hang from the ceiling and sweep their fire across the lane; hatches open in the floor and the ceiling; firewalls run from ceiling to floor. Where the arrows flow up or down, a draft shoves you that way.

Copper traces

The motherboard's traces are wide and the virus is slow, so learn the turned keys here. A bright pit in the copper is a via, and it spits sparks; a dark crack lets Bit Mites crawl out. Halfway round, a silver jumper wire bridges the board to the next trace down: hold Right on it to hop a lap early.

The ribbon cable

Stay on the cable: the BLASTER can't fly off its edges onto the board. Packets swoop onto your line just ahead of you and dive straight down it, so keep firing along the cable. Crosstalk waits by the top edge and jumps across: speed up or slow down to let it pass. The cable is worn, too. Where the gray is split open the colored wires inside show, and the bright one in the middle of each split spits sparks; ride past on the far side. Some nicks let Crosstalk crawl out. In two places a strip of gray tape joins two coils across the board: hold Right on it to hop onto the next coil a lap early. Miss it and you only ride one more lap.

The 555

That breadboard on the motherboard runs on a 555 timer, and so does the firewall just past it. Red LED on? Beam on. Wait for the blink.

pages.head: The Stages
pages.html:
The Stages

Every stage flies the same loop: A straight up, B right (side-on), C back down, D back left (side-on): round the stage's edges. Then E cuts corner to corner through the middle, and F is the boss. Stages 2 to 5 open with a ride down the data bus, seen from behind, toward the chip the stage is in. A card before each run tells you what is new.

  • The Motherboard. The Data Bus, Expansion Slots, The Chipset, The Drive Cage and Copper Traces. Green fiberglass, light green traces, capacitors, transistors, the BIOS chip and somebody's homemade 6502 on a breadboard. Learn to fly here: first straight up the data bus, then side-on along the board past expansion cards standing in their slots, then back down through the chipset's turrets, hatches and firewalls, then back left under the drive cage, where the IDE cable hangs low. Last, corner to corner along four wide copper traces (the silkscreen counts them, 3, 2, 1) to the BIOS chip.
  • Memory Lane. The Memory Bus, The Address Bus, The Memory Bank, The Cache, Stack Overflow and The Ring Buffer. First the memory bus to the DRAM chip, one interrupt or Parity Bat at a time, then two. Then data streams start shoving you around, Leak Slugs come looking for you, and the 6502's stack fills page one a byte at a time. Then side-on between two memory sticks, where the stack hangs from the upper one and fills toward the floor; back down the lane between the cache chips; and back left under three stacks. Last, a ring buffer: four rows of memory corner to corner, from TAIL round and round to HEAD.
  • The Sound Card. The ISA Bus, The Big Name, The Waveform, The Woofer, The Mixer and The Score. First out the expansion slot down the ISA bus to the FM chip, with Note-heads and stray bits in the lanes. Then up the face of the card itself, a Sound Boaster, from its gold edge fingers past SOUND BOASTER in letters you could read from across the room. Then side-on through the song as the oscilloscope draws it, the wave swinging the floor and the ceiling up and down. Back down the card, when a big speaker thumps, the middle of its cone kicks the BLASTER on: ride the beat! Back left across the mix, Note-heads dance in conga lines and records spin. Last, the song the FM chip is playing, written out as five staves of music corner to corner, from the treble clef to the final bar.
  • The Hard Disk. The IDE Bus, The Platter, Between Platters, Bad Sectors, The Spindle and Fragmented File. First the IDE bus to the drive, where the Skulls come two at a time. Then the platter spins under you in wide streams. Then side-on through the thin gap between two spinning platters, where the read/write arms seek in and out; back down through bad sectors, where Tanks cut across the lane; and back left to the spindle, with arms reaching in from both platters. Last, follow Mom's recipe file, scattered over the disk in four fragments, from its directory entry corner to corner round to EOF.
  • The CPU. The Local Bus, The Pipeline, The Heat Sink, The Core, The Cooling Fan and The Ribbon Cable. First the local bus, the fastest in the box, straight at the 486 with Opcodes and interrupts every half a second. Then everything at once, faster, inside the 486 itself. Then side-on over the chip, weaving the heat sink's fins; back down through the core, where the Leak Slugs hunt fast; and back left under the cooling fan, its draft pushing down where the heat pushes up. Last, the hard disk's ribbon cable, a wide gray band of thin wires with a red stripe along pin 1, coiled corner to corner over the board. Each lap of the screen ends at the kink, where the cable bends flat and carries you round onto the next coil down; the numbers printed on it count the coils, 4, 3, 2, 1, to the plug at the far end, where GLITCH is waiting.

pages.head: The Bosses
pages.html:
The Bosses

At the end of every stage the screen stops scrolling and a boss blocks the only way out: a glowing gate in the top wall. The boss's weak points sit right in the gap. They glow, they turn red as they crack, and they burn the BLASTER badly if you touch them. Shoot them until they burst, then fly up through the hole.

  • The BIOS Bug has clamped onto the BIOS chip. Its jaws sweep, its sides spit seekers. Shoot out its eyes, then its crown.
  • The Memory Leech has its mouth over the exit and its body coiled around the arena. Shoot through the coils.
  • The Feedback Howler hides behind a sliding grille. Fire through the gaps, then slip through after.
  • The Head Crash is the hard disk's read head, gone rogue, with rings of platter shards orbiting it.
  • GLITCH itself. You'll see.

pages.head: Credits and Registering
pages.html:
Credits

Design, art, music and programming: Claude.

Made with GAME-MAKER 2.0 by Recreational Software Designs. Every scroll, every shot and every boss in Virus Blaster is plain Game-Maker. No programming!

Registering

Virus Blaster is shareware. Copy it for your friends, upload it to your favorite BBS, put it on a shareware disk. If you enjoy it, please register for $15. Registered pilots receive:

  • the BLASTER Hint Book, with the red film for peeking at one answer at a time;
  • a full-color poster of GLITCH;
  • our thanks, and news of our next game.

Send a check or money order (US funds) to:

Sandbox Software

Dept. BLAST

P.O. Box 000

Pittsburgh, PA 15213

This is a fictional address made up for this game; there is no real Sandbox Software to mail. Please do not send money anywhere.

Remember: scan every download!

printables.pitch: GLITCH is eating the family 486! Shrink down and blast your way to the CPU in a real scrolling shoot-'em-up.

keys.Up: Speed ahead flying up, brake flying down (W too)
keys.Down: Brake flying up, speed ahead flying down (S too)
keys.Left: Strafe left (A too); side-on, speed ahead or brake; a lane over on the bus
keys.Right: Strafe right (D too); side-on, speed ahead or brake; a lane over on the bus
keys.Space: Nova Bomb: five plasma bolts (one charge)

items.title: BLASTER Hint Book
items.note: Answers hidden: use the red film
items.intro: Stuck on a stage? Find your question, lay the red film over the answer, and read only as much as you need. GLITCH is counting on you giving up. Don't!

hints.q: How do I shoot?
hints.a: You already are! The twin guns fire every third tick whenever the BLASTER moves, and it is always moving forward. Just steer under the virus.

hints.q: The screen won't scroll backward.
hints.a: It never does. The arrow pointing back only brakes. Dodge sideways, and push the arrow the way you fly to rush past trouble.

hints.q: Which way does each run fly?
hints.a: Every stage flies a loop: A up, B right, C down, D left, then E corner to corner through the middle to the boss. The ship on the card before each run faces the way you will go.

hints.q: When should I use a Nova Bomb?
hints.a: On bosses, and on a heavy that is about to run you over. The big middle bolt hits hardest, so fire it from right under the target.

hints.q: How do I see my energy?
hints.a: Press F2. It shows your energy (40 when you start), your spare ships, and your Nova charges as counter 5.

hints.q: Turrets keep shooting me no matter what.
hints.a: Shoot the armored collar off: three hits. The turret burns out into a smoking wreck that never fires again, and you get 250 points.

hints.q: How do I get past a firewall?
hints.a: Wait until it blinks off and fly through. If you must go through a live one, you burn a hole in it but lose 6 energy for each block you touch.

hints.q: What is the red light on the breadboard?
hints.a: The clock LED on a 555 timer. It keeps time for the homemade 6502 and for the firewall right past it. LED on, beam on. LED off: go!

hints.q: Now I am flying sideways!
hints.a: Expansion Slots (1-B) is seen from the side. Up and Down climb and dive, Right speeds ahead and Left brakes. Cards stand up from the board and the IDE cable hangs from the drive cage: fly over one and under the other.

hints.q: Now the board scrolls down!
hints.a: That's The Chipset (1-C), flown back down the board. Down speeds ahead, Up brakes, Left and Right strafe, and the guns fire down at the virus coming up. The gate signs count the screens left.

hints.q: And now I'm flying left?
hints.a: The Drive Cage (1-D) is side-on again, back the other way. Left speeds ahead and Right brakes. The IDE cable hangs lower here: pick your height a cable ahead.

hints.q: The screen went corner to corner and my keys feel wrong.
hints.a: On the copper traces the keys turn with the track. Up speeds you along the trace, Down slows you, Left steers toward its top edge and Right toward its bottom edge. Keep to the middle of the copper and let the guns do the work.

hints.q: The trace ends at the edge of the screen and starts again!
hints.a: It bends flat and comes round the wrap as the next trace down. That is the way on. The silkscreen counts the traces left, 3, 2, 1, and the last one runs into the chip. A silver jumper wire halfway round bridges to the next trace: hold Right on it to save a lap.

hints.q: The BIOS Bug's head won't break.
hints.a: Shoot its two eyes (the bottom half of the head) first; they take 9 hits each. Then the crown (6 each). Fly up through the hole where the head was.

hints.q: Now I see the BLASTER from behind and it won't shoot!
hints.a: That's the Memory Bus, a ride between stages. The guns are cold on the bus. Left and Right hop a lane; stay out of the lanes the interrupts and Parity Bats come down. When the sign reads BUS: 0, steer into the middle lane and it carries you into the DRAM chip.

hints.q: Something keeps pushing me sideways.
hints.a: Data streams: the rows of flowing arrows. Steer the other way while you cross, or hold Up to cross faster.

hints.q: A row of bytes keeps closing across the lane.
hints.a: That's the 6502's stack in page one. It fills from $01FF on the right, then overflows and empties all at once. Hug the left side and slip through, or wait for the pop.

hints.q: The slugs follow me everywhere.
hints.a: Leak Slugs never give up. They take three hits; shoot them as they come at you from ahead, because they are slower than you and can't catch up from behind.

hints.q: Between the memory sticks, the stack shuts on me.
hints.a: It hangs from the upper stick and fills one byte at a time toward the floor, then pops. Stay low and slip through the gap under it, or wait for the pop. The chips stick up from the lower board and hang from the upper one, so pick your height early.

hints.q: On the way back there are three stacks!
hints.a: Stack Overflow (2-D). Each fills toward the floor a byte at a time, then pops. Stay low and slip under, or brake and wait for the pop: Right brakes when you fly left.

hints.q: Where does the ring buffer end?
hints.a: At HEAD. You start reading at TAIL, and each row bends flat at the kink and wraps round onto the next one. The big numbers count the rows left: 3, 2, 1. The dotted cyan pointer on the way round jumps you a row early if you hold Right on it.

hints.q: I can't reach the Memory Leech's mouth.
hints.a: Its coils soak up your shots. Each segment pops with one hit, so clear a few, then fire up through the gap at the mouth.

hints.q: Which lane is safe on the ISA Bus?
hints.a: Watch under the chip on the horizon: everything starts there as a dot and slides down its own lane. Two hazards at once always leave one lane open. The green 1s and 0s are stray bits; they hurt less than an interrupt, but they still hurt.

hints.q: Something keeps rolling across the board from the left.
hints.a: Sound waves from the line-out jacks on the card's bracket. Each one rolls along a faint trace with arrows on it, so you can see its lane coming. Cross between two waves, or shoot one to break it up.

hints.q: Why is that chip laughing at me?
hints.a: It's the FM music chip, and its maker printed YO MAMA! HA HA HA right on it. The HAs fly out of its bottom corners. Shoot the collar off each corner (three hits) to shut it up.

hints.q: The floor and ceiling keep moving up and down.
hints.a: In The Waveform they are the song itself, drawn by the oscilloscope. Follow the swing a little ahead of time: climb before a rise, dive before a dip. It gets louder (wider) toward the end.

hints.q: What do the big speakers do?
hints.a: When a speaker thumps out, the middle of the cone kicks the BLASTER on the way it is flying, down the card in The Woofer (3-C). Use it to rush past a crowd.

hints.q: Note-heads are dancing at me from the left side!
hints.a: That's The Mixer (3-D), flown left. The conga lines peel off one after another; keep to the middle and let the guns meet them. Shoot the spinning records from far off: they burst.

hints.q: The music is all over the screen!
hints.a: That is The Score, the song the FM chip is playing. Ride each staff corner to corner; it bends flat and wraps onto the next one, and the measure numbers count the staves left: 4, 3, 2, 1. The final double bar is the way out, and a tie on staff 2 hops you a staff early if you hold Right.

hints.q: The Feedback Howler's grille blocks everything.
hints.a: The bars slide two blocks each way. Fire when a gap lines up with the face, and slip through a gap the same way when the face is gone.

hints.q: On the IDE Bus the Skulls come two at a time.
hints.a: Pick the open lane while they are still small dots, and hop early: a hop takes a moment to finish. The bar beside the sign shows how much of the ride is left.

hints.q: The platter keeps throwing me around.
hints.a: The wide streams of The Platter push hard. Hug the side the stream pushes you toward so you can't be shoved into a turret.

hints.q: Something keeps reaching across the gap between the platters.
hints.a: The read/write arms, seeking. Each one reaches in, burning like a firewall, then pulls back out. Wait for it to pull back, or fly over or under it.

hints.q: How do I stop a Tank?
hints.a: Six hits. They drive straight, so get out of the way first and shoot from the side as they pass.

hints.q: On the way to the spindle the arms come from both sides.
hints.a: In The Spindle (4-D) an arm reaches in from each platter at once. They pull back together: cross between them then, or brake (Right, flying left) and wait.

hints.q: Where am I going on the slanted tracks?
hints.a: Following Mom's recipe file. It lies in four fragments over the platter: ride each one corner to corner, round the kink onto the next, 3, 2, 1, to EOF. The gold chain on fragment 2 is a cluster link: hold Right on it to jump a fragment early.

hints.q: The Head Crash's shards are everywhere.
hints.a: They orbit in two rings at different speeds. Wait between the rings, and fire straight up when the middle is clear.

hints.q: The Local Bus is too fast for me!
hints.a: Hop one lane at a time and start as soon as you see the dots. Grab the repair capsule if your energy is low. At 0 the middle lane lights up and pulls you into the 486: be in it.

hints.q: This run is all fins and hot air.
hints.a: That is the heat sink over the 486. Fins rise from the bottom and the fan's grille hangs from the top, so pick your height a fin ahead. Where the arrows climb, the heat shoves you up: let it carry you over the next fin.

hints.q: Under the fan I keep getting pushed down.
hints.a: That's the fan's draft, where the arrows fall, in The Cooling Fan (5-D). The heat still pushes up where they climb. Ride one and fight the other.

hints.q: The ribbon cable goes on forever!
hints.a: It is coiled, and it loops on purpose. Each lap of the screen ends at the kink, where the cable bends flat, and round the bend you are on the next coil down. The numbers printed on the cable count the coils left: 4, 3, 2, 1. The plug at the end of coil 1 is the way out, and GLITCH is waiting past it. Just keep riding.

hints.q: Which way is which on the cable?
hints.a: The keys turn with the track. Up speeds you along it, Down slows you down, Left steers toward its top edge (mostly up) and Right toward its bottom edge (mostly right).

hints.q: Something keeps zapping me near the colored stripes.
hints.a: Those are splits in the insulation, with the wires inside showing. The bright spot in the middle of each one spits sparks up toward the cable's top edge. Ride past on the bottom side, or speed through.

hints.q: Is there a shortcut?
hints.a: Two strips of gray tape join one coil to the next across the board, one on coil 4 and one on coil 2. Hold Right as you pass one and you slide over onto the next coil, a whole lap early. Miss it and you just ride one more lap.

hints.q: How do I beat GLITCH?
hints.a: Its brain sits behind a sliding grille in its face. Stay in the middle, fire through the gaps, and watch out for the Leak Slugs that hunt you from the bottom corners. Grab the repair in the bottom-left corner when you need it. When the brain bursts, it isn't over: two bare cores still plug the way out, and two fast shards come hunting. Keep firing and keep moving.

hints.q: Is there a secret ending?
hints.a: Reboot the PC clean and you'll see it. Then try for a better score!

hints.q: Some say the felt-maker left something behind. Where?

items.to: To every caller who downloaded COOLGAME.ZIP last week:
items.body:
I owe you all an apology. Somebody uploaded COOLGAME.ZIP to the Games area on Tuesday, and I posted it without scanning it. It was not a cool game. It was GLITCH.

If your hard disk light hasn't stopped blinking, if your homework is full of little purple skulls, or if your high scores have turned into gibberish: you have it too.

I'm told the only cure is VACCINE.EXE and a pilot with steady hands. I have neither. I hear you do.

From now on every upload gets scanned. Every one. Good luck in there.

news.head: Game-Maker learns to scroll
news.html: Sandbox Software's Virus Blaster is a real vertically scrolling shoot-'em-up, built entirely in Game-Maker. The trick? The BLASTER drifts forward two pixels on every frame of every move, so the screen has no choice but to follow it up the map.

news.head: Scan every download
news.html: Virus Blaster starts with a mistake: late one night you download COOLGAME.ZIP from a BBS you never called before, and it turns out to be GLITCH, a virus that eats a PC from the inside out. Shrink down and blast your way up through the family 486: five stages, twenty-five scrolling runs and five bosses. It's only a game, but the moral is real. Scan every download.

news.head: Since last issue: Watt made it home
news.html: Ohm Sweet Ohm players have been rewiring the Bitmores' Smart Home all spring. The most-asked question on the BBS: why can't Watt roll on a slant? Circuit boards are wired in straight lines, and so is Watt. The most-pressed key, by a mile, is R for reboot. It costs a spare battery, and the board starts over exactly as it was.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: The SysOp's assistant
news.html: The SysOp checks every upload for viruses before it goes in the file area, and he has help: a corgi named Teddy, who sleeps under the desk with his chin on the modem cable. This month Teddy walked across the keyboard twice and posted one message to the board. It read "jjjjjjjjj". It is our most popular message.

news.head: In the workshop: A hundred worlds
news.html: Our biggest game yet is on the workbench, and it's big on purpose: we want to find out how much Game-Maker can hold. A courier, a galaxy chart, five sectors and eighty-eight worlds to land on, every one of them wrapping all the way around. It's called Maximus: The Hundred Worlds. It needs a 386. Sorry, 286.

news.head: Readable from across the room
news.html: Overcreative Labs says you can read the name on a Sound Boaster from across the room. Virus Blaster put that to the test. On the sound card, in the run called The Big Name, the BLASTER flies up the face of the card, over SOUND BOASTER in letters two blocks tall. The FM chip carries its maker's name too: YO MAMA! HA HA HA. It laughs. Modest is still not on the board.

news.head: Letters: "My clock radio plays polka"
news.html:
"My clock radio plays polka at three in the morning, just like the Bitmores'. Is my house haunted?" - A reader in Ohio

The Scoop replies: Check for lightning. Then send for Watt.

blurb: Two short levels about blocks that take turns. Gates stand in a row, and each one is open for only a short while. A ring of blocks, each turning into the next after a few ticks, decides whose turn it is, and a row of lamps shows it: the lit lamp is the open gate. manual.title: KEEP IT BRIEF! The Tiny Pockets Library

pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
KEEP IT BRIEF!

The Tiny Pockets Library

Behind the little red door of The Dog House, a little lending library on a post with a dog-bone handle and a paw-print knob, is a library much bigger than the box. Nobody is sure how. The librarians have stopped asking.

Every book on its shelves holds exactly one hundred words. Not ninety-nine. Not one hundred and one. The Word Counter, a brass adding machine the size of a desk, makes sure of it.

Last night the Word Counter jammed. It said 99. Then 101. Then STOP. And every word fell out of every book.

You are Mystery Robot Joe, the night librarian: a tin robot with a red bow tie, reading glasses he does not need, and a tally counter where his heart would be. Step into each book, pick its hundred words up off the floor, and put thirty-two stories back together before the morning patrons arrive.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type BRIEF and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster plays the music, the page flutters and the shushing; without one, the PC speaker does its best impression of a librarian.

A cartoon plays first: the night the words fell out. Press any key for the menu, then pick Play. Leave the menu alone and Joe will give you a tour of the reading room himself.

Keys

Arrows, W A S D or the number padWalk one step (hold to keep walking)
F1Help
F2Status: it counts the words you are carrying. Words are money. Ask any author.
SpacePocket a small thing. Joe's pockets are tiny, and almost nothing in a library fits in them. Almost.
F5 / F6Save / load
EscBack to the menu

There is nothing to press to use things. Walk into a door, a book or a page, and it does what doors, books and pages do.

pages.head: The Library
pages.html:
The Library

The night is told in four chapters of two wings each: 1. Clowns and Clones (Clown Alley, the Laboratory), 2. Out of Doors (the Docks, the Backyard), 3. Home After Dark (the Living Room, After Hours) and 4. Somewhere Else, Someday (Other Dimensions, the Future Shelf). Every book's cover page says where you are, such as Chapter 2 of 4, book 3 of 8.

The reading room has a door for each of the eight wings. Chapter 1's doors are open; a later chapter's doors are barred, with a tag that names the chapter, until the chapter before it is stamped done in the Reserve Stacks. Over every door is a brass plate inked with that wing's library stamp, the one that stamps SHELVED on its returns. Nobody on staff will say who keeps re-inking them. (Gwinn. It is Gwinn. Look at her paws.)

  • Clown Alley: no running with scissors, or in slow motion
  • The Laboratory: please do not feed the ooze
  • The Docks: pirates, flutes and a paddle wheeler
  • The Backyard: street lights, clotheslines and a very well-equipped Santa
  • The Living Room: thunder (allegedly) and a broken light bulb
  • After Hours: the quiet ones, and an owl who asks whom
  • Other Dimensions: fancy catnip, Escher stairs and a superhero with his underwear on the outside
  • The Future Shelf: books from a strange year called 2026. Who is ChatGPT?

Each wing's hallway has four tall books standing on its shelves, numbered I to IV. Walk into a spine and in you go. The door marked OUT goes back to the reading room.

pages.head: Inside a Book
pages.html:
Inside a Book

Every book is a little world, acted out by whoever was in the story: clowns, professors, pirates, a ficus. Its words lie all over the floor as slips of paper torn from the page:

1a word
5a phrase
10a sentence
20a paragraph (they are short paragraphs)

There are exactly one hundred words in every book. Pick them all up.

THE END is a book with a brass lock reading 100. It will not open for ninety-nine. When you carry a hundred, walk into it: it takes them, opens, and the gold bookmark behind it puts the story back where it belongs. Then the story itself is yours to read, every word of it, and a picture of how it turns out.

THE END is the only way out of a book. In the last three wings, a brass turnstile marked 20 (a word lock) guards a corner of one book: it turns only while you carry twenty words, and the floor behind it hands them straight back. Pick up what you can reach first. Nothing in a book can take your words away, so you can always finish it. Take your time. The patrons are not due until morning.

pages.head: Shushers and Other Hazards
pages.html:
Shushers and Other Hazards

Nothing in the library can hurt a tin robot, and nothing can take his words. Plenty of things in it can fine him.

Shushers are the gray, bun-haired ghosts of librarians past. Touch one and she fines you a point off your score for every moment you stay in her way. Shhh.

Some books bring their own: the scissors in Clown Alley, static electricity in the balloon gallery, the reporters who want a quote, the exceptions thrown at those who call in the Church of the First of Zero. They all fine you the same way. A perfect night's work is 3,200 points: one for every word put back, and not one fine.

Some visitors are harmless: Doc Leo, a hobo clown with a rubber chicken on a leash; Teddy, a corgi who knows left from right; the two Sallys; a tour guide. And Gwinn, who is not allowed in the library and is in the library.

pages.head: The Reserve Stacks
pages.html:
The Reserve Stacks

The purple STAX door in the reading room leads to the Reserve Stacks: staff and robots only. A corridor runs past eight brass stamp gates, one for each wing, each topped with that wing's stamp and a little plate that reads 4.

A gate opens once its wing has four stories stamped SHELVED, and it lets you through without keeping any of them. The Word Counter checks; it does not collect.

Past each pair of gates, a stamp desk (CH1, CH2, CH3) waits in the shelves below the corridor. When both of a chapter's wings are done, walk through their gates and step onto its desk: the chapter is stamped done, a page tells you what you put back and what comes next, and the next chapter's doors in the reading room are open. It is a good moment to press F5 and save.

What is past the gates? The staff say it is exactly one hundred words long. They will not say which hundred.

pages.head: About the Stories
pages.html:
About the Stories

The thirty-two stories in this library are 100 Word Stories by Lewis Moten, reprinted word for word. He wrote every one of them for Laurence Simon's weekly 100 Word Stories challenge on the 100 Word Stories Podcast: a topic each week, exactly one hundred words each, from 2009 to 2014 and again in 2026. Laurence set the early topics; since then each week's winner, voted for by the podcast's listeners, chooses the next one, so the topics on the story cards are theirs. Every story card shows the date it went up, the challenge's week number, and the week's topic.

The challenge signs off the same way every week, and so does this manual: ...And, as always, keep it brief!

Two of the stories, The Interest We Lost and Church of the First of Zero, first went up under the name Mystery Robot Joe. He has a job now.

Only the typography has changed: a 1994 PC has no curly quotes, so they are straight, and an ellipsis is three dots. The Word Counter checked every story. It found one hundred words in each. It found ninety-nine in Steam-Powered Summer, until somebody pointed out that a hyphen makes two words into one word, or one word into two, depending on whom you ask. It is still thinking about it.

pages.head: Credits
pages.html:
Credits

Stories: Lewis Moten, written for Laurence Simon's weekly 100 Word Stories challenge on the 100 Word Stories Podcast

The weekly topics: Laurence Simon and the podcast's writers and listeners, whose weekly winners chose the next topic

Game design, art, music and every block of the library: Claude Opus 5.5

Starring: Mystery Robot Joe, the night librarian; the Word Counter, as itself; Teddy the corgi; Gwinn; Doc Leo, PhD (Comedic Science); and a great many shushers

Published by Sandbox Software. Shareware: copy it for a friend, and return it on time. Register for $10, exactly.

Parked out front: THE CHEZ, the CitiCar, plugged in at its rear passenger-side charge port. It is always charging.

Made with Game-Maker 3.0 from Recreational Software Designs.

No words were harmed in the making of this game. A few were fined.

items.title: A note from the Word Counter
items.note: Found taped to the inside of the box lid
items.address: Reading Room Desk, The Tiny Pockets Library, behind the red door of The Dog House
items.body:
Joe,

I jammed. I am not proud of it. I said 99. Then I said 101. Then I said STOP, which is not even a number. By the time I came to, every word had fallen out of every book on every shelf.

Here is what I need. Every book holds one hundred words. I will open THE END of a book for exactly that many, and not one fewer. Pick them up off the floor. All of them. The slips say how many words each is worth; I am told some of them are paragraphs. Short paragraphs.

The shushers mean well. They will still fine you, a point at a time. So will the scissors, the static, the reporters, and a twister I would rather not discuss.

When four stories are back in a wing, that wing's stamp gate in the Reserve Stacks will let you through. I check. I do not collect. Do the wings two at a time, a chapter of the night each; when a chapter's two are done, go through their gates and stamp it on its desk, and I will open the next chapter's doors. Past the gates there is one more book. Do not ask me what is in it. I only count.

THE END is the only way out of a book. Nobody can take your words in there, so you can always finish. Finish.

items.title: Librarian's Hint Book
items.note: Answers hidden: use the red film
items.intro: Stuck? Find your question, then slide the red film over the answer. The Word Counter would like you to know it disapproves of hints. It disapproves of most things.

hints.q: THE END won't open. I picked up every word I could see.
hints.a: Press F2: it counts the words you carry. Every book has exactly 100, and nothing can take them, so if it says less there is a slip you missed. Look behind the furniture and along the edges.

hints.q: THE END opened, but nothing happened.
hints.a: Walk onto the open page, then onto the gold bookmark right behind it. The bookmark puts the story back.

hints.q: Why did my score go down?
hints.a: A fine. Shushers, scissors, static and the like cost a point a moment while they touch you. A perfect night is 3,200.

hints.q: Which door goes where?
hints.a: Top row, left to right: Clown Alley, the Laboratory, the Docks, the Backyard. Bottom row: the Living Room, After Hours, Other Dimensions, the Future Shelf. The purple STAX door on the right goes to the Reserve Stacks.

hints.q: Some doors have brass bars across them.
hints.a: Those wings belong to a later chapter. Finish the chapter you are in (both of its wings, four books each), then go to the Reserve Stacks, walk through its gates and step onto its stamp desk. The next chapter's doors open.

hints.q: Can I fix the Word Counter?
hints.a: You fix it by filling the books. It will keep flipping between 099, 101 and STOP until then. It is a very dramatic machine.

hints.q: The stamp gates won't open.
hints.a: Each gate wants four stories restored in its own wing. The plate on the gate says 4. It means it.

hints.q: Where do I stamp a chapter done?
hints.a: In the Reserve Stacks, past the gates of the chapter's two wings: the desk marked CH1, CH2 or CH3 in the shelves just below the corridor. Step down onto it. Then save with F5.

hints.q: What is the thirty-third book?
hints.a: Exactly one hundred words. Whose hundred is up to you.

hints.q: Some say there is a felt egg somewhere in the library.
hints.a: Libraries lose things. Good libraries keep a lost and found. The Word Counter complains that nobody can find it.

hints.q: Where is the lost and found?
hints.a: In the Reserve Stacks. Not every shelf there is as solid as it looks: look for a book pulled half out, with a red ribbon hanging from it.

hints.q: I found it. Now what?
hints.a: Walk onto the shoebox and press Space. Finders, pocketers. F2 shows it in Joe's pocket, and a save keeps it there.

hints.q: Step by step?
hints.a: In the Reserve Stacks, walk to the bottom right corner, past the fern, and keep walking right into the shelf with the ribbon. In the Lost and Found, stand on the shoebox with the egg and press Space. Leave by the OUT door.

hints.q: Clown Alley: the scissors keep getting me.
hints.a: They run a loop inside the ring. Wait at the curb until they pass, then walk. Do not run. Do not run in slow motion either.

hints.q: The Future Shelf: how do I get the tea?
hints.a: You don't. Nobody does. That is the story.

hints.q: The Backyard: why do the street lights come on?
hints.a: They are on timers, one after another. Spooker Boy never noticed them. Now you have.

news.head: A library in a box on a post
news.html: Our lawyers asked us to keep the press release for KEEP IT BRIEF! under one hundred words, so: thirty-two stories, one hundred words each, a tin librarian who refuses to round, and shushers who fine. Register for $10. Exactly $10. The Word Counter will not make change. Keep it brief.

news.head: Since last issue: Nobody has spoiled it
news.html: Final Curtain detectives: thank you for keeping the solution off the BBS. Commissioner Hale has handed out a lot of strikes this month. The most-asked question is about Victor's safe: three dials, four symbols, no numbers. Victor never wrote anything down that he could hang on a wall instead. Go and look at his walls.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: Neighbors on the line
news.html: We aren't the only game-makers on the 412 exchange. Over on The Sofa BBS (1-412-555-SOFA), The Bard of Bizarre has been uploading song-games, each one built around a song of his. It's a different shop with a different sense of humor, and we like it a lot. Tell the SysOp we said hi. Meanwhile, THE CHEZ is parked in front of the library in this game. Of course it's charging.

news.head: In the workshop: Real depth
news.html: The office 486 has been running all night for weeks, ray tracing chrome spheres, glass cubes and one red teapot. That's our next game: Depth Perception, where every scene has a near plane and a far plane, and only the one in focus is solid. No cardboard glasses required.

news.head: Letters: "Is Macbeth the cat a suspect?"
news.html:
"Is Macbeth the cat a suspect? He was in every room I searched." - A detective, by modem

The Scoop replies: Not a suspect. Macbeth is the theater cat, and he goes wherever he likes. Most cats do.

It's 3 AM at Sandbox Software, and the render of the century is 99% done. Then COUNT POLYGON creeps in through the modem and starts stealing polygons. Spheres go octagonal. The teapot goes square.

pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
DEPTH PERCEPTION

Sandbox Software, Pittsburgh. 3:00 in the morning.

The render of the century is crawling down the monitor one scan line at a time: the box art for Depth Perception, a perfect checkerboard running to the horizon, chrome spheres, a glass cube, a red teapot and the morning sun coming up behind them all. It has been rendering for eleven hours. It is 99% done. Everybody went home. Doc Leo, our lighting director, left his spotlight on.

Then COUNT POLYGON crept in through the modem.

The Count lives on polygons. He took the gold sphere's and left it an icosahedron. He took the teapot's and left it a brick. He spread his henchmen through every scene of the render: wireframes that were never finished, jaggies made of nothing but stair steps, and polygon bats.

He missed one. RAY, the chrome sphere from every ray tracing demo ever made, still has every polygon he was born with. Roll him through six scenes, collect the red, green and blue lenses, and get him to each scene's vanishing point, where all the parallel lines meet. The box art goes to the printer at nine.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type DEPTH and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster plays the music and the digitized sound effects; without one, the PC speaker beeps along. Every picture in the game was rendered ahead of time, so a 386 plays it as well as a 486.

From the menu, pick Play. Leave the menu alone for half a minute to watch a demonstration. Read Storyline shows how the night went wrong; Read Instructions is a short version of this manual.

Light and lives

Ray runs on light. He starts with 100 and three lives. Henchmen, steam and bats cost light; light bulbs, friends and THE CHEZ's charge port give it back. Fall into the void and the render of Ray simply falls apart: you start that scene over, with every lens you have found still in your pocket. Press F2 to see your score, light and lives.

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

↑ ↓ ← →
or W S A D		Roll. Ray stops when you let go - he's a very well-behaved sphere.
Q E
keypad 7 9 1 3		Roll diagonally: Q up-left, E up-right; the number pad corners go all four ways.
SpaceFire a ray of light the way you last rolled. It renders a wireframe into a crystal (touch the crystal for points) and takes faces off Count Polygon.
F1-F6Help, status, music on/off, sound on/off, save, load.
EscQuit to the menu.

A joystick works too: push to roll, button 1 fires.

pages.head: Pulling Focus
pages.html:
Pulling Focus

Every scene in the render has two planes: the near plane and the far plane. A camera can only focus on one at a time, and in Depth Perception that is the whole trick:

Sharp things are solid. A blur isn't there.

Near blocks are amber; far blocks are cyan. When the near plane is in focus, amber blocks are crisp and solid and cyan ones are soft, see-through blurs you can roll right through. Pull focus to the far plane and it's the other way round.

Focus rings

Roll onto a focus ring (a chrome ring set in the floor) to pull focus to the other plane. The lens inside the ring glows the color of where it will take you. Ray's own bands tell you which plane is in focus: amber near, cyan far.

Glass walkways

Glass walkways are only there in their own plane: an amber walkway holds you up when the near plane is in focus and is just a blur over the void when it isn't. Violet auto-focus panels drift in and out of focus on their own; wait for them to sharpen, then roll. A panel flickers pink twice just before it blurs out, so a flicker means stay put.

A fresh render

Pulling focus re-renders the scene the way it was: photons and bulbs come back, and gates close again. The lenses you've found stay with you.

pages.head: Things in the Render
pages.html:
Things in the Render

PhotonA little star of light: 25 points.
Light bulb30 light in the first two scenes, 20 in the next two and 15 in the last two: the closer the render is to done, the scarcer light gets.
Red, green and blue lensesOne of each in every scene. The RGB gate before the vanishing point takes one of each.
RGB gateThree glass doors in a row: red, green, blue. Each opens only for its lens.
Vanishing pointThe white light at the end of each scene.
SlopesGolden chevrons in the Fractal Peaks pull you the way they point. Ride them down; don't ride them into a pit.
TeapotsThe Utah teapot, the most rendered object there is. In the Teapot Temple they puff steam at you.
THE CHEZA 1976 1/2 CitiCar, plugged in on the rear passenger side. Push against its charge port for light.

pages.head: Friends and Fiends
pages.html:
Friends and Fiends

Friends

Teddy, a Pembroke Welsh corgi with a big grin, strolls the Checkerboard. Gwinn, sitting pretty in her pink collar, keeps the Glass Garden. Doc Leo, our lighting director (fedora, green tie, red sneakers and a rubber chicken on a leash), paces the Teapot Temple. Bump into any of them for a little light. Henchmen that bump into them get rendered.

Fiends

WireframesNever finished. One ray renders them into crystals.
JaggiesAliasing with teeth. They hop along their beat.
Your dark doubleThe Hall of Mirrors' reflection that rolls at you when you get close.
SteamFrom the teapots. Hot.
Polygon batsThe Count's, from their nests at the vanishing point.
ShardsThrown by the four prisms in Count Polygon's arena. A prism glows pink just before it throws. Shards are slow and a ray shatters them.
COUNT POLYGONTwenty faces of vampire. He swoops round you and dives. A ray cracks him, a second shatters him, a third takes faces off: twenty, then eight. When the eight are gone he coughs up the blue lens he swallowed and flees into the far plane, where he waits with four faces, then a triangle, then a point. What he leaves behind opens the last door.

pages.head: The Six Scenes
pages.html:
The Six Scenes

1. The Checkerboard. Where every render begins. Learn to pull focus.

2. The Glass Garden. Crystals, glass tiles and auto-focus panels over the void.

3. The Hall of Mirrors. Nine rooms joined by near doors and far doors, around a middle room drawn isometrically, as if the camera had swung round to a corner. Which one of you is real?

4. Fractal Peaks. Infinitely detailed, mostly downhill. The plateau at the top is seen isometrically, amber blocks standing a tier taller than cyan.

5. Teapot Temple. A colonnade, three shrines, an isometric sanctum around the vanishing point and a parked CitiCar.

6. The Vanishing Point. Where all parallel lines meet, and Count Polygon waits in an arena drawn isometrically: amber near cubes stand a full tier tall, cyan far cubes half that. Beat him in the near plane, then follow him up through the blue gate into the far plane.

pages.head: Tips from the Render Farm
pages.html:
Tips from the Render Farm

  • Look before you roll: if a block is soft and see-through, it isn't there right now.
  • A focus ring always drops you off on its far side. Step back onto it to pull focus back.
  • A lens boxed in by blocks of one color is a puzzle, not a wall: find the ring that turns that color to a blur.
  • Fire before a wireframe reaches you: a rendered crystal is worth points; a bump costs light.
  • The auto-focus panels keep time. Count it while you wait on solid ground.
  • Lost a life? The scene starts over, but your lenses don't.
  • Count Polygon doesn't move until you come within reach. Pick your spot first, and keep a cube between you and the prisms.
  • He swoops to one side, then the other, then dives. Line up as he swings by, and roll clear when he dives.
  • Not every mirror in the Hall of Mirrors is a wall.

news.head: We threw away the cardboard glasses
news.html: Our art department spent a week squinting through red and blue cellophane before Doc Leo said what everybody was thinking: real depth isn't two colors, it's focus. Depth Perception has a near plane and a far plane in every scene, and only the one in focus is solid. The glasses are still in the box. You won't need them.

news.head: How long does a render take?
news.html: Every block, sprite and cartoon in Depth Perception was ray traced on our office 486. The intro alone took a long weekend. The box art took eleven hours and a vampire. We are told the next machine will be faster.

news.head: Since last issue: The Word Counter is still thinking
news.html: KEEP IT BRIEF! readers have put a lot of stories back together this month. The Word Counter found exactly one hundred words in each one but Steam-Powered Summer, where it found ninety-nine until somebody pointed out what a hyphen does. It is still thinking about it. Judging by the BBS, so are some of you.

news.head: Around the Sandbox: Our lighting director
news.html: Doc Leo has a new title. He spent so many nights at the office watching renders crawl down the screen that we made him our lighting director, which mostly means he leaves the spotlight on. He paces the Teapot Temple with his rubber chicken, Teddy strolls the Checkerboard, Gwinn sits pretty in the Glass Garden and THE CHEZ is parked in the temple, charging. Gwinn's sit is ray traced. We're counting it.

news.head: In the workshop: We are getting around to it
news.html: Since our first disk you've asked for a role-playing game, and since our first disk we've said we'd get around to it. We're getting around to it: Quest for the Round Tuit, a whole kingdom where everything gets done, eventually. Towns, dungeons, a quest log, and a horseless carriage you may recognize.

news.head: Letters: "A corgi in my library book"
news.html:
"I found a corgi in one of the library books. Is that allowed?" - A reader, by mail

The Scoop replies: Teddy is allowed. Gwinn is not allowed in the library, and is in the library.

items.title: Depth Perception Hint Book
items.note: Answers hidden: use the red film
items.intro: From the render farm's log book. Lay the red film over an answer to read it - the only red glasses this game will ever ask you to wear.

hints.q: How do I get past a wall of amber blocks?
hints.a: Amber blocks are the near plane. Find a focus ring with a cyan lens and roll onto it: the far plane comes into focus and the amber blocks turn to blurs you can roll through.

hints.q: I pulled focus and now I'm stuck.
hints.a: Every focus ring works both ways. Step off it and back onto it to pull focus back. You arrive on the far side of the ring each time.

hints.q: Why did the photons come back?
hints.a: Pulling focus re-renders the scene the way it was. Photons, bulbs and gates come back; your lenses stay in your pocket.

hints.q: Where is the red lens?
hints.a: Behind the column of amber blocks. Pull focus at the ring left of the column and roll straight through.

hints.q: How do I cross the chasm?
hints.a: In the near plane the amber walkway holds you. Roll onto the ring in the middle: the far plane comes into focus and the cyan walkway takes you the rest of the way.

hints.q: The violet panels keep disappearing under me.
hints.a: They drift in and out of focus together, about two seconds each way. Wait on solid ground until they sharpen, then roll without stopping. A pink flicker means a panel is about to blur out: don't step on.

hints.q: The green lens is across three sets of panels.
hints.a: The middle set keeps the opposite time to the others. Cross one set, wait on the little island for the next to sharpen, and go again.

hints.q: Which doors can I use?
hints.a: Amber doors open in the far plane, cyan doors in the near plane. The ring in the middle room pulls focus.

hints.q: My double keeps rolling into me.
hints.a: It wakes when you come close. Face it and fire first: one ray renders it to nothing.

hints.q: The green lens is boxed in by cyan blocks.
hints.a: Cyan blocks are solid in the far plane, the only plane that gets you into that room. Roll onto the ring beside the box: in the near plane the box is a blur. Take the lens, then step back on the ring to get out.

hints.q: The arrows carried me away!
hints.a: Golden chevrons pull you the way they point until you hit something. Ride the two chutes on purpose; stay off the slopes beside the pit.

hints.q: The blue lens is boxed in by amber blocks.
hints.a: You cross the glass bridge in the near plane, where amber is solid. The ring in that room pulls focus to the far plane, where the box is a blur. Take the lens and ride the ring back.

hints.q: I'm low on light.
hints.a: THE CHEZ is plugged in at the parking lot. Stand below its rear wheel and push up against the charge port: it charges you, and keeps charging.

hints.q: The steam keeps getting me.
hints.a: A ray puts out a puff. Keep moving past the teapots rather than standing beside them.

hints.q: How do I beat Count Polygon?
hints.a: He waits until you come within reach, then swoops: to one side of you, to the other, then straight at you. Line up with him across or down the arena, turn to face him and fire. A ray cracks him, a second shatters him and a third takes faces off. When his eight faces are gone he coughs up the blue lens he swallowed and flees into the far plane: take the lens, roll through the blue gate at the top of the arena and finish him there.

hints.q: Purple shards keep hitting me.
hints.a: The four prisms in the arena throw them, a little faster in the far plane. A prism glows pink just before it throws. Shards are slow: roll away, put a cube between you, or shoot them.

hints.q: The last door won't open.
hints.a: It wants the last polygon the Count leaves behind in the far plane. Roll over it, then go through the gold door and the red and green gates.

hints.q: Somebody felted something into the render...
hints.a: Not every mirror in the Hall of Mirrors is a wall. Look for a mirror with something faint inside it.

hints.q: I found a mirror I can roll through. Now what?
hints.a: Behind it is the Prism Egg on a pedestal. Roll onto it and press Enter to pick it up and keep it. Leave by the mirror just above the one you came in by.

hints.q: Just draw me a map.
hints.a: In the far plane, go up through the amber door into the top middle room, then right into the top right room past the red lens. Its right wall has two two-way mirrors; with the far plane in focus, roll through the lower one, then press Enter on the felt egg.

title: Diagonal Wrap
author: Claude
blurb: One map, one road, laid two ways. The map wraps: walk off the bottom and you come in at the top. In level 1 the road runs straight down and wraps once. In level 2 it is tilted a little, so it wraps three times and is three times as far on the very same map. Signs in the levels say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and tilt a road of your own.

box.back: A small explorer in a purple beanie follows a road between hedges. The map wraps at every edge: walk off the bottom and you come in at the top. Laid straight, the road wraps once. Tilted a little, the same road goes round three times and is three times as far. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and tilt a road of your own.
features: Level 1 runs straight down the map and wraps once; level 2 is the same road tilted, so it wraps three times
A dashed line marks the map's edge on the road
Signs in the levels count the laps and the length

title: Everybody Talks
author: Claude
blurb: Two short rooms about talk with more than one voice. Walk into a friend and one picture comes up with everyone in it, a speech bubble for each turn and a name over each, and the words fit the bubbles. Level 1 is a talk of two; level 2 is a group of four across two cards. Signs in the levels say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change who says what.

box.back: A small explorer in a teal beanie crosses two short rooms of signs and friendly faces. Walk into a friend and a whole talk comes up in one picture, with a speech bubble and a name for each voice, then back to the room. Read the signs, listen in, then open the game in Game-Maker and change who says what.

title: Roll the Dice
author: Claude
blurb: One short level about chance. A die sits on the ground, rolling: it is a ring of six blocks that each turn into the next after a few ticks. Mara walks into it and it stops on the face it shows, handing over a gold key for an odd face or a silver key for an even one. A wall ahead has a gold door on the ground and a silver door up a ladder, so the face picks the door. Signs in the level say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change how long a face shows.

box.back: A small explorer in a green beanie finds a die rolling on the ground. Touch it and it stops, and the face it shows hands over a key: gold for odd, silver for even. Two doors wait ahead, one for each key. The game has no random number: the tick decides the roll. Play, then open the game in Game-Maker and change how long a face shows.

title: Drop Down
author: Claude
blurb: Two short tunnels about a monster that falls. Monsters have no gravity in Game-Maker, so a friend sits on a crate until you hit the crate twice and it breaks, then its Movement, a step down walked again and again, takes it down. Plop is solid and drops into a dip fast; Pip is soft and drifts down slowly. Signs say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change how fast a friend falls.

Plop falls fast and blocks the way; Pip drifts down slowly and is soft to walk through. Play, then open the game in Game-Maker and change how fast a friend falls.

title: Kit Ducks
author: Claude
blurb: Two short levels about dodging by ducking. Friendly bluebirds fly back and forth at the height of Kit's head, and Down makes them duck: their crouch has a picture in the bottom block only, so a bird in the row of their head touches nothing. A ball rolling on the ground is another matter, and needs a hop. Signs explain each idea, and every level has a page on how it is made.

box.tagline: Down, and the bird flies over.
box.back: A small explorer in a teal beanie has two levels to cross. Friendly bluebirds patrol at the height of their head, and a low awning stops them hopping over. Hold Down and they duck, and the bird passes with nothing to touch. In the second level a ball rolls along the ground, and a duck does not help: it needs a hop. Signs say what each level shows, and the manual says how each is made.

title: Fireworks Night
author: Claude
blurb: Fireworks drawn with monsters. A monster can turn into another monster when its path ends, so a rocket that flies up turns into a burst at the top, and the burst turns back into the rocket: two monsters taking turns make a firework that never stops. Level 1 has two launchers, each on its own time, and Enter launches a rocket of your own. Level 2 is a show over a sleeping town: rings, peonies and willows, each burst nine monsters on one path, each launcher with its own time so no two go off together. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change a burst.

box.back: An explorer in a red beanie watches the night sky. A rocket is a monster on a path up; when the path ends it turns into a burst, and when the burst has fallen it turns back into the rocket. Nine bursts on one path make one big one, and launchers with their own times seldom go off together. Read the signs, press Enter to launch your own, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a burst.

title: Flash Safe
author: Claude
blurb: Three short levels about making a game that is easy on the eyes. Some players can get sick from fast flashing, and some people have seizures from flashing light, so a game should never rely on it. Level 1 shows a hit without a flash: a beep, an ouch face, a number that rises and fewer hit points. Level 2 blinks a small amber lamp once a second and pulses another in soft steps. Level 3 lifts a dark sky a little, holds it, and lets it settle. Signs and still pictures show the wrong way, and the simple rules: no more than 3 flashes in a second, no big red flashes, keep flashing small, and offer other cues. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change a time.

box.back: A small explorer in a red beanie has three short rooms that show how to make a game that never relies on a flash. A hit gets a beep, a face, a number and fewer hit points. A warning lamp blinks slowly and small. A storm sky lifts a little and holds. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a time.
features: A hit shown four ways, and none of them a flash
A lamp that blinks once a second and one that pulses softly

title: Flicker and Flow
author: Claude
blurb: Things that flicker and flow in place, drawn with blocks. A block can turn into another block a few ticks later, so a loop of blocks is an animation, and how it feels is in its times. Level 1 is a castle hall: torches whose flame pulses on even times, then flickers on uneven ones, and flags whose wave steps along two blocks. Level 2 is a cliff with a waterfall four blocks wide, with a lip, a body and a splash that are each a loop. Level 3 is a fire on a hill and the sparks it throws. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and change a time.

box.tagline: Flames that flicker, flags that wave, water that falls.
box.back: A small explorer in a red beanie walks a castle hall, a cliff and a hilltop. A block can turn into another block a few ticks later, so a loop of four makes a flame, a flag or a waterfall move. Even times give a steady wave or a falling stream. Uneven times and frames that lean give a flicker. One block means one clock, so two loops keep neighbors apart. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and change a time.
features: Level 1 shows a torch that pulses, one that flickers, and flags that wave
Level 2 is a cliff with a waterfall made of three kinds of loop
Level 3 is a fire on a hill with sparks that rise
Signs in the levels say how it is done

title: The Giant
author: Claude
blurb: Two short levels about a boss that is really several monsters. A monster is one block, so a giant is four standing together: Rocky, made of stone, fills a narrow way with the exit door behind her, and each part pops on its own. A star flies level with Rima's hand, so the head needs a step to stand on. In level 2 a tin robot takes two hits a part: after the first it blinks red for a moment and a star goes right through, so you wait. Signs in the levels say how. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and look at the parts.

box.back: A small explorer in a teal beanie has a pocketful of gold stars and two short levels to cross. Rocky, big, grumpy and made of stone, fills a narrow way to the door, but a monster is only one block, so she is really four, and each pops on its own. Then a tin robot blinks red when it is hit, and a star goes right through it. Read the signs, press Enter, wait your turn, then open the game in Game-Maker and look at the parts.
features: Signs in the levels explain each idea

title: Third Goat from the Left
author: The Bard of Bizarre
blurb: Bethlehem, the holy night. You are the goat nobody painted: eat your way out of the shepherds' fold, scream your fainting cousins stiff, get lost in the crowd, dodge the wise men's camels and take your place in the line at the manger, third from the left. Shareware from The Sofa BBS, based on the song by The Bard of Bizarre, one of his bizarre gospels (lyrics shaped by ChatGPT from Lewis Moten's prompt; recording and cover art made with Riffusion, now Google Flow Music).
